title: Dakdoritang
subtitle: Spicy braised chicken with potatoes and carrots
excerpt: A hearty Korean one-pot of bone-in chicken thighs braised in a spiced gochujang and soy sauce broth with potatoes and carrots. The sauce reduces to a thick, glossy coating as the chicken becomes tender. Serves 4 in about 50 minutes.
sourceNotes: Dakdoritang, also known as dak bokkeum tang in some parts of Korea, is a beloved home-cooking dish that became widespread in the mid-twentieth century as gochujang production was industrialised and became affordable to most households. The combination of chicken, potato, and a deeply spiced sauce makes it one of the most comforting dishes in the Korean repertoire.

glossaryTerms.definition: Gochugaru is Korean red chilli powder made from sun-dried red peppers. It ranges from mild to hot and has a slightly smoky, fruity quality distinct from generic chilli flakes. It is used in enormous quantities in Korean cooking, colouring soups and stews a vivid red and providing warmth without the sharp bite of some other chillies.

Braising is a cooking method in which food is first seared or cooked briefly over high heat, then simmered slowly in a small amount of liquid in a covered pot. The liquid reduces and concentrates during cooking, creating a rich sauce. In Korean cooking, braised dishes are called jjim or jorim depending on the technique, and often include soy sauce, chilli paste, and aromatics as the braising liquid.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 50 minutes including prep. Dakdoritang is a Korean

dish where bone-in chicken thighs cook slowly in a punchy sauce of gochujang, soy sauce, garlic, and ginger alongside chunky potatoes and carrots. As it simmers, the sauce reduces to a thick, glossy coating that clings to everything.
The heat level here depends largely on how much

you use. Start with a tablespoon for a mild result and increase from there. Adding the spring onions right at the end keeps them green and fresh against the deep red sauce. Use bone-in thighs wherever possible as they stay moist through the long cook and add depth to the braising liquid.

items.prepNote: bone-in, skin-on, cut into large pieces

content.text: Put the chicken pieces in a large bowl. Add the gochujang, gochugaru, soy sauce, garlic, ginger, sesame oil, and sugar. Mix well. Leave to marinate for 15 minutes at room temperature, or overnight in the fridge.
Add the chicken pieces to the pot and turn to coat. Bring to the boil over medium-high heat.
Once boiling, reduce the heat to medium, cover, and cook for 15 minutes.
Add the potatoes and carrots. Stir to submerge in the sauce, adding a splash more water if the pot looks dry. Cover again and cook for a further 15 minutes.
Remove the lid and increase the heat to medium-high. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce reduces and thickens to a glaze.
Check the chicken is cooked through and the potatoes are tender. Drizzle with sesame oil and scatter over the spring onions. Serve immediately with steamed rice.

items.symptom: The sauce is too thick and catching on the bottom
items.cause: The heat was too high during the covered cooking phase or too little water was added
items.fix: Add 50ml water and stir immediately. Reduce the heat to low and continue cooking covered

items.symptom: The potatoes are cooked but the chicken is still pink at the bone
items.cause: Large bone-in pieces take longer to cook than expected
items.fix: Add another 10 minutes covered on medium heat. Check the thickest piece by cutting to the bone before serving

items.symptom: The dish tastes flat despite all the spices
items.cause: The sauce needs more salt or acidity to lift the flavours
items.fix: Add another tablespoon of soy sauce and a small pinch of sugar. Taste again after 2 minutes of further simmering

content.text: Dakdoritang is a family meal dish across Korea. It appears at weeknight dinners and on cold weekend afternoons when something warming and filling is wanted. The one-pot format means it travels well to shared tables and works for large groups simply by scaling up. Leftovers reheat particularly well, with the sauce becoming even more concentrated and flavourful the next day. It is always served with rice to soak up the sauce.
